paragraphs.heading: Why the largest ones matter
paragraphs.text: A volcanic eruption throws lava, volcanic bombs, ash and various gases out of a volcanic vent and fissure. Many eruptions endanger only the area right around them. Earth's largest eruptions are different. Their impact can be regional or even global, and some affect the climate and contribute to mass extinctions.

paragraphs.heading: Two kinds of eruption
paragraphs.text: Eruptions can generally be sorted into two kinds. Explosive eruptions are sudden ejections of rock and ash. Effusive eruptions are relatively gentle outpourings of lava. In an explosive eruption the magma is driven out by a rapid release of pressure, often with the explosion of gas that had been dissolved in the material. The most famous and destructive eruptions in history are mainly explosive.

paragraphs.heading: How big explosive eruptions get
paragraphs.text: Explosive eruptions usually involve thick, highly viscous magma that is high in volatiles such as water vapor and carbon dioxide. An eruptive phase can be a single eruption, or several spread over days, weeks or months. The eruption at Lake Toba 74,000 years ago threw out at least 2,800 cubic kilometres. The Yellowstone eruption 640,000 years ago produced around 1,000 cubic kilometres. Eruptions of that size happen somewhere in the world every 50,000 to 100,000 years.

paragraphs.heading: Slow but not harmless
paragraphs.text: An effusive eruption is a steady outpouring of lava, not a set of large explosions. It can last for years or decades and produce extensive flows of fluid lava. Kīlauea on Hawaiʻi erupted continuously from 1983 to 2018. In that time it produced 2.7 km³ of lava, which covered more than 100 km². Effusive eruptions can look benign, yet they can be as dangerous as explosive ones.

paragraphs.heading: Laki, Iceland, 1783–1784
paragraphs.text: One of the largest effusive eruptions in history was that of Laki in Iceland in 1783–1784. It produced about 15 km³ of lava. One fifth of Iceland's people were killed by it. The disruption to the climate that followed may also have killed millions elsewhere. Two Icelandic eruptions were larger still: Eldgjá around 934, with 18 km³ of lava, and Þjórsárhraun around 6700 BCE, with 25 km³. The second of these is the largest effusive eruption of the last 10,000 years.

paragraphs.heading: Flood basalts
paragraphs.text: In the past, large igneous provinces, as they are called, went through highly active periods of volcanism that produced huge oceanic plateaus and flood basalts. One of these provinces can be made up of hundreds of large eruptions and millions of km³ of lava in total. No large flood basalt eruption has happened in human history. The most recent was over 10 million years ago. In the geologic record they are often linked with the breakup of supercontinents such as Pangea, and they may have contributed to a number of mass extinctions.

paragraphs.heading: What the record leaves out
paragraphs.text: There have likely been many more eruptions of this scale in Earth's history than the ones on record. Erosion and plate tectonics have done their damage, and many eruptions did not leave geologists enough evidence to work out their size. Even for known eruptions, the estimated volume can be quite uncertain. Most large igneous provinces have not been studied thoroughly enough, or are not preserved well enough, for the size of their individual eruptions to be established.
